lessons.title: Settler Pressure: Railroads, Cattle, Gold and the Indigenous Plains

before.content_html:
A Cumulative Pressure

By 1850 the Indigenous peoples of the Plains had spent two centuries adapting to a horse-and-buffalo culture. By 1880 that culture had been almost destroyed. The story is not a single catastrophe. It is the story of three settler pressures — the railroad, the cattle industry and gold prospecting — stacking on top of each other, each one renewing the assault on land, food and treaties already weakened by the one before. For the 8-mark Analytical Narrative question, students need to see this as a chain, not a list.

Underneath all three pressures ran a fourth: US government policy, which kept funnelling Plains nations onto smaller and smaller reservations, paid for in unreliable annuities, and policed by Indian agents who often skimmed the food and supplies before they reached the people they were meant to serve.

Key Fact

Three settler pressures combined to destroy Plains Indigenous life: railroads split the buffalo herds and ferried hide hunters; the cattle industry took the grass and water; gold strikes broke treaty lines that were supposed to be permanent. Each renewed the pressure on a shrinking territory.

Railroads as Buffalo-Killers

The First Transcontinental Railroad, completed in 1869, did not just carry passengers; it physically split the great buffalo herd into northern and southern populations that never recombined. After 1870 a new generation of high-velocity rifles and the demand for tanned hides from eastern leather factories turned the bison into a commodity. Rail companies hired contracted hunters to feed crews — William ‘Buffalo Bill’ Cody killed an estimated 4,280 bison in eighteen months supplying the Kansas Pacific.

From the trains themselves, sport shooters fired into the herds for entertainment as carriages rolled past. From around 1872 hide hunters operated in teams across the southern plains, killing the southern herd by 1875. The northern herd followed by 1883. From an estimated 30 million bison in 1800, fewer than 1,000 wild animals remained by 1890. General Philip Sheridan endorsed the slaughter as a deliberate strategy: “Let them kill, skin and sell until the buffalo is exterminated, as it is the only way to bring lasting peace and allow civilisation to advance”. Without the bison, Plains nations lost food, clothing, shelter and the centre of their spiritual life.

Cattle on the Open Range

As the bison disappeared, the open range filled with cattle. The same grass that had fed the buffalo now fed the longhorn herds of John Iliff, Charles Goodnight and the eastern-funded ranches that spread across Wyoming, Montana and the Dakotas through the 1870s and early 1880s. Cattle competed for water at the same rivers and creeks the buffalo had used. Ranchers wanted Plains grass cleared of bison entirely, which they regarded as a competitor for forage.

For Indigenous peoples confined to reservations, the result was a double loss. Their hunting territory was now privately stocked with cattle they were not allowed to take, and the federal beef rations promised under treaty — sometimes spoiled, often short — were a poor replacement for the buffalo herds that had once moved through their lands. Hunger pushed nations off reservations to hunt; that hunting brought them into conflict with ranchers and the army; conflict justified further restrictions. The cycle worked against them at every step.

Weaker answers refer to ‘the Sioux’ as if all Plains nations were one. They were not. The Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Crow and Pawnee had distinct languages, leaderships and very different relationships with the US Government. The Crow scouted FOR Custer at Little Bighorn against their Lakota rivals; the Pawnee fought as US Army auxiliaries on the central Plains. The 2026 specification deliberately uses ‘Indigenous peoples’ to underline this diversity. In a Q3 importance answer, naming a specific nation (the Lakota, the Cheyenne) signals up-to-date subject literacy and unlocks higher bands.

Gold Strikes That Broke Treaty Lines

No settler pressure broke treaty lines as quickly as gold. In the summer of 1858 prospectors found gold near Pike’s Peak in present-day Colorado — on land guaranteed to the Cheyenne and Arapaho under the 1851 first Fort Laramie Treaty. Within a year, around 100,000 prospectors had crossed those hunting grounds; the slogan ‘Pike’s Peak or Bust’ rolled across the Mississippi. The federal government answered not by enforcing the treaty but by writing a new one in 1861 that took back most of the territory it had previously guaranteed.

The pattern repeated. In 1862 the prospector John Bozeman blazed a trail north from the Oregon Trail to the new Montana goldfields, cutting straight through the Lakota Powder River country. Red Cloud’s War (1866–68) was fought to close it. In 1874 a US Army expedition under George Armstrong Custer confirmed gold in the Black Hills of Dakota — territory recognised as Lakota under the 1868 second Fort Laramie Treaty just six years earlier. Within months around 15,000 prospectors had poured in. The treaty collapsed; the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876) followed; and the cycle covered in Lessons 11 and 12 began.

The June 2022 examiner report flagged that students regularly mix up the two Fort Laramie Treaties — an error that caps Q3 answers at the lower band. The 1851 first treaty was a multi-nation council, organised by the US Indian agent Thomas Fitzpatrick, that recognised hunting territory and promised annuities in return for safe passage on the Oregon Trail. The 1868 second treaty ended Red Cloud’s War, closed the Bozeman Trail, and granted the Black Hills to the Lakota. Different decades, different leaders, different outcomes. A useful memory hook: 1851 was about access (a peace council), 1868 was about ownership (a Lakota victory). Every gold-strike sentence in this lesson runs against ONE of those treaties — never both at once.

US Policy: Reservations, Annuities and Indian Agents

Underneath the railroad, cattle and gold pressures, the US policy of annuity payments and concentration onto reservations was failing on its own terms. Reservations shrank with each treaty revision. Annuities arrived late, short, or spoiled. The Indian agents who managed the rations and supplies were political appointees, often unsupervised, frequently corrupt — the agent Andrew Myrick’s 1862 remark that hungry Santee Sioux farmers should “eat grass” helped trigger Little Crow’s War in Minnesota that summer.

By the late 1870s, dependence on government rations — with the buffalo gone, the open range fenced and the Black Hills overrun — was the daily reality of Plains life. Concentration was failing because each new wave of settler pressure renewed the squeeze on the same shrinking territory. For the 8-mark Analytical Narrative question, examiners reward students who chain the four pressures together, not students who list them.

Key Fact

Three gold strikes broke three treaty lines: Pike’s Peak (1858–59) overran Cheyenne and Arapaho hunting grounds promised in the 1851 first Fort Laramie Treaty; the Bozeman Trail goldfields (1862–63) cut Lakota Powder River country; and the 1874 Black Hills strike broke the 1868 second Fort Laramie Treaty — triggering Little Bighorn in 1876.
before.exam_tip_html: For the 8-mark Analytical Narrative question, the summer 2024 examiner report capped students at the lower band when they wrote “three paragraphs that do not link”. Treat the impacts as a CHAIN: railroads split the herds and ferried the hide hunters → the buffalo collapsed → cattle took the grass and water → gold strikes tore up the treaties that were supposed to protect what was left → reservations and Indian agents could not feed the survivors. Use causal connectives (‘because’, ‘led to’, ‘with the result that’) at every paragraph break. Stay inside any dates the question gives you — the 2022 examiner report flagged that students writing about the 1860s lost time on a question dated 1876–1890. Use the 2026 spec wording ‘Indigenous peoples’ to signal up-to-date subject literacy.

lessons.title: Indian Wars: Little Crow, Sand Creek and Red Cloud

before.content_html:
Three Wars in Six Years

Between 1862 and 1868 the Plains shifted from uneasy treaty-making into open war. The first Fort Laramie Treaty of 1851 had promised annuities in return for safe passage across Indigenous land. Within a decade those promises had collapsed under settler pressure, gold rushes and broken supply lines. Three conflicts — Little Crow’s War in Minnesota (1862), the Sand Creek Massacre in Colorado (1864) and Red Cloud’s War in Powder River country (1866–68) — tell the story of why. Each one ended differently, but together they set the pattern for every later confrontation between the US Army and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.

Key Fact

Three Plains wars between 1862 and 1868: Little Crow’s War (1862, Minnesota) ended in the largest mass execution in US history; the Sand Creek Massacre (November 1864) killed about 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho under a US flag; Red Cloud’s War (1866–68) ended in a rare Indigenous victory written into the second Fort Laramie Treaty.

Little Crow’s War, 1862

In the summer of 1862 the Santee Sioux of Minnesota were starving. Their Indian agent had withheld the annuities promised by treaty, and traders refused credit until federal money arrived. When Santee leaders begged the agent Andrew Myrick for food, he reportedly replied that they could ‘eat grass or their own dung’. Within weeks the chief Little Crow led an uprising that killed about 500 settlers across the Minnesota River valley. Myrick himself was found dead with his mouth stuffed with grass.

The US response was overwhelming. Federal troops crushed the rising within five weeks. A military commission tried 392 Dakota men in trials that often lasted only minutes; 303 were sentenced to death. President Lincoln, reviewing the cases personally, reduced the list to 38. On 26 December 1862 those 38 men were hanged together at Mankato — the largest mass execution in US history. The remaining Dakota were stripped of their Minnesota reservation and pushed west to Dakota Territory. Little Crow himself was shot the following summer while picking berries in Minnesota; his scalp was displayed for years afterwards.

The Sand Creek Massacre, November 1864

In Colorado, gold strikes around Pikes Peak had pulled tens of thousands of miners onto Cheyenne and Arapaho hunting land guaranteed by the 1851 treaty. By 1864 the territorial governor John Evans was pressing for war, and Indigenous raiding had hardened settler opinion. The Cheyenne peace chief Black Kettle brought his people to camp near Sand Creek in eastern Colorado, having been told by Fort Lyon’s commander that they were under US protection. He flew both an American flag and a white flag of truce above his lodge.

Just before dawn on 29 November 1864, Colonel John Chivington led around 700 Colorado Volunteers in a surprise attack on the camp. Roughly 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho were killed, the great majority of them women, children and elderly people. The bodies were mutilated; soldiers paraded scalps and severed body parts through Denver theatres in the days that followed. Black Kettle survived, dragging his wounded wife from the creek bed. He would be killed four years later at the Washita River, again under a US flag.

Weak answers refer to ‘the Plains Indians’ or ‘the Sioux’ as if every Indigenous Plains people had the same languages, leaders and aims. They did not. The Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Crow and Pawnee had distinct languages and separate political histories. Some allied with each other; others fought each other. The Crow and Pawnee, for example, often scouted for the US Army against their Lakota and Cheyenne rivals — including at the Little Bighorn in 1876. When you write about the 1862–68 wars, name the specific nation involved (Santee Sioux at Mankato, Cheyenne and Arapaho at Sand Creek, Oglala Lakota under Red Cloud) rather than ‘the Indians’.

Reaction to Sand Creek

Sand Creek divided opinion sharply. A federal investigation in 1865 condemned Chivington’s attack as ‘a foul and dastardly massacre’, but he had already left the army and was never prosecuted. Eastern newspapers and Quaker reformers were appalled; Western newspapers more often praised the Volunteers as having delivered ‘just punishment’. The Cheyenne, Arapaho and allied Lakota launched a wave of raids across the central Plains throughout 1865. The most lasting consequence was political: Sand Creek made it clear that ‘peaceful’ treaty arrangements offered no real protection, and it pushed many younger Indigenous leaders — including the Oglala Lakota war leader Red Cloud — towards organised armed resistance.

Red Cloud’s War, 1866–68

In 1862 Congress had passed the Pacific Railroad Act and prospectors had struck gold in Montana. The fastest route to the new diggings ran north from the Oregon Trail along the Bozeman Trail, straight through the Powder River country — prime Lakota hunting ground guaranteed by the 1851 treaty. The US Army began building three forts (Reno, Phil Kearny, C.F. Smith) to protect the trail in 1866. Red Cloud, an Oglala Lakota war leader, walked out of the negotiations and declared war.

For two years a coalition of Oglala, Hunkpapa, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors blockaded the trail. The decisive moment came on 21 December 1866 outside Fort Phil Kearny, when Captain William Fetterman led a relief column of 80 men out of the fort against orders. He had reportedly boasted that with eighty soldiers he could ride through the entire Sioux nation. Crazy Horse and a small decoy party drew Fetterman’s column over a ridge and into a waiting ambush of about 1,000 warriors. Every man in the column was killed inside half an hour — the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until Little Bighorn ten years later.

The June 2022 examiner report named this confusion as one of the most common errors on questions about the early Plains wars. The first Fort Laramie Treaty (1851) was a multi-nation council organised by the Indian agent Thomas Fitzpatrick: the US recognised tribal territories, promised annual annuities, and guaranteed safe passage on the Oregon Trail. The second Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) was the peace settlement that ended Red Cloud’s War: the US closed the Bozeman Trail, abandoned the three forts, and recognised Lakota ownership of the Black Hills and the ‘unceded’ Powder River country. Pin the dates: 1851 = annuities and safe passage; 1868 = forts abandoned and Black Hills granted.

The Second Fort Laramie Treaty, 1868

Faced with mounting army losses, public pressure and the cost of garrisoning forts that could not be safely supplied, Washington opened peace negotiations in 1868. The terms were extraordinary. The US Army would close the Bozeman Trail and abandon Forts Reno, Phil Kearny and C.F. Smith. The Great Sioux Reservation was set aside for the Lakota, including the sacred Black Hills. The Powder River country was recognised as ‘unceded Indian territory’ into which no white person could pass without Lakota consent. Red Cloud refused to sign until the forts were physically burned. The Lakota set fire to Fort Phil Kearny themselves as the soldiers withdrew.

The 1868 treaty was a rare Indigenous victory written into US law. But it was fragile. When gold was struck in the Black Hills in 1874, Washington moved within two years to force the Lakota off the very land it had just guaranteed them — the path that led directly to the Battle of the Little Bighorn in 1876. Red Cloud’s War WON the treaty; the Black Hills strike unwound it.

Key Fact

Red Cloud’s War (1866–68) ended with the US Army closing the Bozeman Trail, abandoning three forts and recognising Lakota ownership of the Black Hills under the second Fort Laramie Treaty — a rare Indigenous strategic victory. Captain William Fetterman’s loss of all 80 men in December 1866 was the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until Little Bighorn (1876).

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Red Cloud’s War (1866–68) for relations between the US Government and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation of the importance of Red Cloud’s War, supported by specific period detail.

Indicative content:
• Red Cloud’s War was the only major nineteenth-century war the US Government settled by accepting Indigenous demands — the second Fort Laramie Treaty (1868) closed the Bozeman Trail and abandoned Forts Reno, Phil Kearny and C.F. Smith.
• Because the US recognised the Black Hills and Powder River country as Lakota territory in writing, the war set a legal benchmark that later treaty-breaking (the 1874 gold strike, the 1876 ultimatum) could be measured against.
• The Fetterman Fight of 21 December 1866 — in which Crazy Horse’s decoy party led Captain Fetterman’s 80 men into ambush — was the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until Little Bighorn, shaking the Army’s confidence in lightly held forts.
• Because the war showed that a coalition of Oglala, Hunkpapa, Cheyenne and Arapaho fighters could close a strategic trail for two years, federal policy shifted towards reservation containment over open military pressure for the rest of the 1860s.
• The treaty fed directly into the conditions of the next decade: when gold was struck in the Black Hills in 1874, the Lakota could point to a federal promise less than six years old — making the resulting Little Bighorn campaign a war over a treaty the Government itself had signed.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1866–68, 21 December 1866, 1868) and specialist vocabulary (Bozeman Trail, Powder River country, Oglala Lakota, unceded territory).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description of the war without explanation of importance for US–Indigenous relations.

Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1862 the Santee Sioux of Minnesota were starving because annuities promised under earlier treaties had been withheld; the agent Andrew Myrick’s reported ‘eat grass’ remark triggered Little Crow’s rising and the killing of around 500 settlers, ending in the Mankato execution of 38 Dakota men in December 1862.
• Because the Pikes Peak gold rush had drawn miners deep into Cheyenne and Arapaho hunting land guaranteed by the 1851 treaty, tensions in Colorado built up across 1863–64 and culminated on 29 November 1864 in Colonel Chivington’s attack on Black Kettle’s peaceful camp under a US flag at Sand Creek — about 150 were killed, mostly women, children and elderly.
• Because Sand Creek made ‘peaceful’ treaty arrangements look worthless, allied Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota raids spread across the central Plains in 1865 and pushed younger Indigenous leaders — including the Oglala Lakota war leader Red Cloud — towards organised armed resistance.
• Because Congress had authorised the Bozeman Trail and the US Army began building forts through Powder River country in 1866, Red Cloud walked out of negotiations and launched a coalition war; on 21 December 1866 Crazy Horse’s decoy party led Captain Fetterman’s 80 men into ambush outside Fort Phil Kearny — the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until 1876.
• By 1868 the cost of garrisoning forts that could not be safely supplied forced Washington to accept terms: the Bozeman Trail closed, the forts abandoned, and the Black Hills recognised as Lakota territory in the second Fort Laramie Treaty — the closing point of a six-year deterioration that had begun with starving Santee in Minnesota.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1862, 1864, 1866, 1868), specialist vocabulary (annuities, Bozeman Trail, Powder River, Oglala Lakota), both stimulus points covered and integrated with own knowledge.
Secure: Narrative covers both stimulus points and uses some causal linkage.
Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.
Emerging: Thin description with little narrative shape.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Sand Creek Massacre (1864) for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:

Indicative content:
• Sand Creek killed around 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho on 29 November 1864 — mostly women, children and elderly — despite Black Kettle flying both a US flag and a white flag of truce; the loss of so many non-combatants weakened the Cheyenne nation in the central Plains for a generation.
• Because the federal investigation of 1865 condemned the attack but no one was prosecuted, Sand Creek showed that ‘peaceful’ treaty status offered no real protection — pushing more Indigenous leaders towards armed resistance rather than negotiation.
• The massacre triggered an immediate wave of allied Cheyenne, Arapaho and Lakota raids across the central Plains throughout 1865, lengthening the cycle of violence that fed directly into Red Cloud’s War.
• Because survivors brought the story north into Lakota territory, Sand Creek hardened the resolve of younger leaders such as Red Cloud and Crazy Horse, who would not trust unprotected camps near US forts.
• Black Kettle’s death four years later at the Washita River — again under a US flag — underlined the pattern Sand Creek had established: peace chiefs who trusted federal protection could be killed without consequence.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (29 November 1864, around 150 killed, federal investigation 1865) and specialist vocabulary (Cheyenne, Arapaho, peace chief, Colorado Volunteers).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.

Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of Little Crow’s War (1862) for relations between the US Government and the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.

Indicative content:
• Little Crow’s War showed how easily withheld annuities could push a treaty-bound nation into open war — the agent Andrew Myrick’s reported ‘eat grass’ remark made it clear that paper guarantees meant nothing without the food and money the treaties had promised.
• Because around 500 settlers were killed in the Minnesota River valley, eastern public opinion swung sharply against Indigenous nations on the Plains, hardening political support for harsher policy and a larger frontier military presence.

• Another consequence was that surviving Cheyenne carried the story north into Lakota country, hardening the resolve of younger leaders such as Red Cloud and Crazy Horse who would refuse to camp unprotected near US forts.

Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

lessons.title: Cattle's End, the Range Wars and Frontier Law and Order

before.content_html:
From Boom to Bust on the Open Range

Through the 1870s and early 1880s the Plains had become a cattle gold mine. The long drives from Texas to Abilene, the new refrigerated railcars and a steady London market for chilled beef pulled British and eastern American investment onto the open range. By 1885 a single Wyoming county might run 100,000 head of cattle on grass that, ten years earlier, had carried buffalo. Speculators talked of doubling money in a season. The land’s carrying capacity was being ignored.

Two warnings were already on the books. Joseph Glidden’s 1874 patent for barbed wire was being strung across homestead claims faster than the cattle barons could buy them out. And the dry summer of 1886 had left grass thin going into the winter. What broke the system was the weather.

Key Fact

The open-range cattle industry collapsed for two linked reasons: ranchers had overstocked the grass during the 1880s boom, and the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 killed 50–90% of cattle in some Wyoming and Montana herds. After 1887 ranchers shifted to smaller, fenced ranches with hay-fed winters — the era of long drives and unbranded mavericks was over.

The Big Die-Up, 1886–87

The winter that began in November 1886 was the worst in living memory on the northern Plains. Blizzards drove temperatures to −40°C across Wyoming, Montana and the Dakotas. Cattle drifted south, piled into draws and froze in their thousands. Some ranches lost 90% of their stock; even careful operators lost half. When the spring thaw came in 1887 the carcasses were so thick along fence lines that contemporaries described whole valleys filled with rotting cattle. British investors pulled their money out within months.

The shape of ranching changed permanently. Ranchers who survived enclosed their land with barbed wire, cut and stored hay through the summer, and bred smaller numbers of higher-quality cattle that could be sheltered in the winter. The era of the long drive ended. So did the era of the unbranded maverick — on a fenced ranch every animal had an owner.

New Farming on the Plains

Alongside the cattle bust, settled farming was finally taking hold. The mechanical reaper and the combine harvester, John Deere’s steel plough that broke the dense Plains sod, refrigerated railcars that shipped grain and beef east, and the huge bonanza farms of the Dakotas turned the High Plains into a wheat-growing region within a decade. The same railroads that had carried cattle north now carried wheat, beef and milk east to Chicago and on to Britain. Farming and ranching no longer competed for the same open grass; barbed wire had separated them.

Hollywood paints the late frontier as ungoverned territory until heroic sheriffs arrived. The reality is more complicated: by 1880 most cow towns and mining camps had paid town marshals, county sheriffs and access to federal courts. The OK Corral was not a fight over an absence of law — it was a fight inside the law, between Earp’s town marshals and the Clantons’ rural cattle interests. Likewise the Johnson County War of 1892 was triggered precisely because the cattle barons could no longer get their way through elected sheriffs and juries. The story of this lesson is the limits of frontier law where money and politics outran it — not its absence.

Showdown Lawmen: Earp, Holliday and the OK Corral

By 1881 Tombstone, Arizona, was a silver-boom town with around 7,000 people and three of the Earp brothers wearing badges. Wyatt Earp was assistant town marshal and a part-owner of saloon and gambling interests. Doc Holliday, the dentist-turned-gambler, was a personal friend. The Clantons and McLaurys were rural cattlemen who had clashed with the Earps over rustling allegations and a stagecoach robbery investigation. On 26 October 1881 the two sides met behind the OK Corral. Around 30 seconds of gunfire left three of the Clanton-McLaury party dead and Virgil and Morgan Earp wounded.

The OK Corral was small — six men, three deaths — but its significance was symbolic. It showed that the difference between ‘lawman’ and ‘outlaw’ on the late frontier was often a question of who held the badge that morning. Earp moved across his career between marshal, gambler, saloon-owner and unofficial enforcer. The legal system in Tombstone struggled to convict either side: a coroner’s inquest cleared the Earps; a follow-up hearing found in their favour again. The Earps left Arizona within a year.

Billy the Kid and the Lincoln County War

Three years earlier, in New Mexico Territory, the same blurred frontier law had produced Henry McCarty — better known as Billy the Kid. The Lincoln County War (1878) was a feud between two rival merchant-rancher factions that had captured the county’s sheriff, courthouse and federal contracts. Billy fought on the losing side. By 1880 he was wanted for the murder of a sheriff and a string of cattle thefts. Sheriff Pat Garrett tracked him to Fort Sumner and shot him there in July 1881. Billy was 21.

Billy’s actual importance was modest — he was one outlaw among many. What made him a national figure was the speed at which the Lincoln County War became a story about how local government could be captured by competing rancher factions, and how the elected sheriff might be the most dangerous man in the room. The OK Corral and the Lincoln County War were the same problem in two states: the official law was now in place, but it was still negotiable for those who had money or guns.

The June 2022 examiner report on the analytical narrative question singled out students who drifted outside the dates the question gave them. A question on the cattle industry 1876–1890 should not start with the 1860s long drives from Texas to Abilene; that material belongs in earlier lessons. Stay tightly inside the timeframe. Within 1876–1890 your chain runs: open-range boom in the early 1880s → British investment and overstocking → thin grass in summer 1886 → the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 → barbed wire enclosure and the smaller fenced ranch by 1890. That is one decade of linkage and the marks live there.

The Johnson County War, April 1892

By the early 1890s the cattle industry had been hit twice over: the Big Die-Up had wiped out winter herds, and homesteaders were claiming and fencing land the cattle barons used to graze freely. In Wyoming’s Johnson County, members of the Wyoming Stock Growers Association believed elected sheriffs and juries were now packed with small ranchers and homesteaders sympathetic to rustlers. They drew up a list of around 70 men they accused of cattle theft and hired around 50 Texas gunmen to ride in and execute them.

The expedition reached Wyoming in early April 1892 and killed two suspected rustlers at the KC Ranch before being surrounded by a hastily organised local posse of 200–300 men. The cattle barons’ force took refuge at the TA Ranch and was only rescued when President Benjamin Harrison ordered the US Cavalry to intervene. Back in court the trial was packed with friendly jurors paid for by the Stock Growers; every defendant was acquitted. The state legislature, dominated by ranchers, blocked any further investigation. The Johnson County War became a national scandal that exposed exactly how far frontier law could be bent when wealth and politics were on the same side.

Key Fact

The Johnson County War (April 1892) saw the Wyoming Stock Growers Association hire 50 Texas gunmen to kill suspected rustlers; only US Cavalry intervention prevented a massacre, and a packed jury acquitted every defendant. The OK Corral (26 October 1881) and the Lincoln County War (1878) had already shown that being on the losing side of a feud could matter more than being inside the law.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Overstocking and the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 ended the open range; ranchers shifted to smaller, fenced ranches with hay-fed winters, and barbed wire (Glidden 1874) replaced the long drive and the unbranded maverick.
  • The OK Corral (26 October 1881) and the Lincoln County War (1878) showed the limits of frontier law: the difference between marshal and outlaw could be a badge or a feud rather than a clear principle.
  • The Johnson County War of April 1892 saw the Wyoming Stock Growers Association hire 50 Texas gunmen against suspected rustlers; only US Cavalry intervention and a packed jury kept it from being a massacre, exposing how far elected law could still be bent for cattle-baron money.

Examiners explicitly warned against drifting outside the dates — do not waste paragraphs on the 1860s long drives from Texas to Abilene; that is earlier-lesson territory. Use causal connectives (‘because’, ‘led to’, ‘this meant that’) and specialist vocabulary (open range, maverick, bonanza farm, barbed wire, range war) so the marker can see linkage rather than narration.

Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• Through the late 1870s and early 1880s the open range looked like easy money; British and eastern investors poured capital into Wyoming, Montana and Dakota herds, encouraged by refrigerated railcars and the London beef market.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 for the cattle industry of the West.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Die-Up killed 50–90% of cattle in some Wyoming and Montana herds, bankrupting many ranches and triggering the immediate withdrawal of British and eastern American investors who had funded the boom.
• Because surviving ranchers could not afford another such loss, the industry shifted to smaller, fenced ranches with hay cut in summer for winter feed — ending the open-range model.
• Because barbed wire (patented by Glidden in 1874) was already being used to enclose homestead claims, the post-Die-Up shift to enclosure was technically straightforward and accelerated rapidly.
• Because the long drive depended on continuous grass between Texas and the railheads, the move to smaller fenced ranches ended the long drive and the era of the unbranded maverick — every animal now had an owner.
• Because the Die-Up bankrupted small operators while leaving large incorporated ranches intact, it widened the gap between cattle barons and small ranchers that fed directly into the Johnson County War of April 1892.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (winter 1886–87, 50–90% losses, 1892) and specialist vocabulary (open range, barbed wire, maverick, range war).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Johnson County War (1892) for understanding law and order on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Johnson County War showed that, even thirty years into Wyoming’s settled frontier, large landowners could still hire 50 Texas gunmen to kill suspected rustlers and outrun the elected sheriff — the elected law could not restrain organised wealth.
• Because President Benjamin Harrison had to order the US Cavalry to break the siege at the TA Ranch, the war revealed that local law on the Plains still depended on federal force to function in extremis.
• Because the trial was packed with friendly jurors paid for by the Wyoming Stock Growers Association and every defendant was acquitted, the case showed how frontier court law could be bent by money and political connections.
• Because the state legislature, dominated by ranchers, blocked further investigation, the war demonstrated that the rise of statehood (Wyoming admitted 1890) had not by itself produced impartial law.
• Because the war became a national scandal — covered by eastern newspapers as a betrayal of frontier ideals — it strengthened the political case for federal grazing reform and the long-term curbing of the cattle barons’ influence.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (April 1892, 50 gunmen, Wyoming Stock Growers Association, Harrison) and specialist vocabulary (range war, packed jury, statehood).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how law and order on the late frontier was tested in the years 1878–1892.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the OK Corral (1881)
• the Johnson County War (1892)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In 1878 the Lincoln County War in New Mexico Territory pitted two rival merchant-rancher factions against one another; both sides used elected sheriffs and federal contracts as weapons, producing the conditions in which Henry McCarty — Billy the Kid — rose as an outlaw before Sheriff Pat Garrett killed him in 1881.
• Because Tombstone, Arizona, by 1881 had a silver-boom population of about 7,000 and rival rural cattle and town saloon interests, the friction between the Clantons and McLaurys and the Earp brothers exploded into the OK Corral gunfight on 26 October 1881 — thirty seconds of fire, three deaths, and two competing legal hearings that cleared the Earps.
• Because the law could not produce a clear verdict in feuds of that scale, frontier disputes increasingly depended on which side held the badge or the better-paid lawyers — even where formal courts were now in place.
• Because the Big Die-Up (1886–87) had bankrupted small operators while leaving large incorporated ranches intact, by the early 1890s Wyoming’s cattle barons faced rising homesteader fences and elected sheriffs they could no longer rely on.
• In April 1892 the Wyoming Stock Growers Association hired about 50 Texas gunmen to kill suspected rustlers in Johnson County; only US Cavalry intervention and a packed jury kept it from being a massacre, completing the story of how late-frontier law could still be bent by organised wealth even after statehood.

Mastering: Sustained narrative with explicit causal linkage, period detail (1878, 1881, 1886–87, April 1892), specialist vocabulary (range war, Stock Growers Association, town marshal), both stimulus points covered.

Developing: Coverage of one stimulus, or both with weak linkage.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of barbed wire for the development of farming and ranching on the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Joseph Glidden’s 1874 patent made fencing the Plains affordable for the first time — cheaper and faster than wood or stone in a region with neither — which let homesteaders enclose 160-acre claims they could not otherwise have defended.
• Because barbed wire enclosed homestead claims, it began separating farming from ranching on what had been continuous open grass; the open-range cattle model was already under pressure before the Big Die-Up.
• Because barbed wire could exclude cattle from rivers and waterholes, it shifted bargaining power towards homesteaders and small ranchers who could now block the long drive and the open-range herd from key water sources.
• Because barbed wire made the smaller, fenced ranch viable, after the 1886–87 winter ranchers could enclose hay meadows and rebuild on a model that did not depend on free grass.
• Because barbed wire reduced the value of unbranded mavericks (every animal on a fenced ranch had an owner), it changed the economics of cattle theft and helped trigger the cattle-baron political backlash that ended in the Johnson County War of 1892.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (1874 patent, 160-acre homestead, 1886–87, 1892) and specialist vocabulary (open range, maverick, range war).
Secure: Two strands explained with relevant detail.
Developing: One strand explained, or two named with limited detail.
Emerging: Description without explanation of importance.

practice_questions.text: Explain two consequences of the ‘Big Die-Up’ winter of 1886–87 for the cattle industry.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks for two separately developed consequences, each linking the Die-Up to a specific feature of the period.

Indicative content:
• One consequence was that surviving ranchers shifted to smaller, fenced ranches with hay-fed winters and higher-quality breeds — the open range and the long drive ended within a few years.
• Another consequence was that British and eastern American investors withdrew their capital from the cattle industry, ending the speculative boom that had drawn outside money onto the open Plains during the early 1880s.

Mastering: Two consequences each developed with linkage to a named feature (e.g. fenced ranching, withdrawal of investment).
Secure: Two consequences identified, one developed clearly.
Developing: Two consequences identified with limited development, or one developed.
Emerging: One consequence loosely identified.

lessons.title: Wounded Knee, the Dawes Act and the End of the Frontier

before.content_html:
The End of a Continent’s Wildlife

In 1850 around 30 million bison roamed the Great Plains. By 1890 there were perhaps 1,000 left. The destruction was driven by three connected pressures: the railroads, which sold seats to hunters and cleared track for shipments; eastern leather demand, which paid handsomely for hides; and the US Army, which under General Philip Sheridan endorsed the slaughter explicitly as a strategy to defeat the Indigenous peoples of the Plains. Sheridan reportedly told the Texas legislature in 1875 that the buffalo hunters had ‘done more in the last two years to settle the vexed Indian question than the entire regular army has done in the last thirty years’.

The collapse of the herd ended the horse-buffalo culture in a generation. Indigenous nations whose food, shelter, fuel, clothing and trade had centred on the bison now depended on government rations on shrinking reservations. The very logic that had let Plains nations stay independent — mobility on horseback after a moving food source — was no longer possible.

Key Fact

Buffalo numbers fell from around 30 million in 1850 to about 1,000 by 1890, driven by railroad-mounted hunters, eastern leather demand and a deliberate US Army strategy endorsed by General Sheridan. The collapse forced Indigenous Plains nations onto government rations on reservations — the food, shelter and trade base of horse-buffalo culture was gone.

Reservations and Carlisle

By the 1870s most Plains nations had been pushed onto reservations far smaller and poorer than the lands they had hunted across. Rations were issued by federal Indian agents, often late and often short. Disease, malnutrition and dependence rose together. Federal policy turned from confining Indigenous peoples to actively reshaping them. In 1879 Captain Richard Henry Pratt opened the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania — the first off-reservation boarding school. His motto was ‘Kill the Indian, Save the Man’: children were stripped of their language, names and clothing, dressed in military uniforms and trained to be farmers and domestic servants. Carlisle became the model for over 25 federal boarding schools that operated for the rest of the period.

The Black Hills and the Battle of the Little Bighorn, 1876

The 1868 second Fort Laramie Treaty had recognised Lakota ownership of the Black Hills. In 1874 a US Army expedition under Custer found gold there. Within months prospectors were pouring in; Washington responded by ordering all Lakota and Cheyenne onto smaller reservations by 31 January 1876. Many bands refused. A coalition under Sitting Bull (Hunkpapa Lakota) and Crazy Horse (Oglala Lakota) gathered in the Powder River country.

On 25–26 June 1876 Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer, leading the US 7th Cavalry, attacked a much larger village along the Little Bighorn River in Montana. Custer split his command into three. His own column of around 210 men was annihilated within an hour by a Lakota and Cheyenne force of perhaps 1,500 fighters. Around 268 US soldiers died in total. The victory was real and shocking, but short-lived: federal forces poured into the Plains over the following five years. Crazy Horse was killed in custody at Fort Robinson in September 1877; Sitting Bull surrendered in 1881 after exile in Canada.

Hollywood inherited a Custer who fought a hopeless ‘Last Stand’ against unstoppable numbers. The reality was more critical of him. Scouts had warned Custer the village was the largest ever seen on the Plains; he chose to attack anyway and split his command into three, weakening every element. Even contemporary US Army reports questioned his judgement. The image of Custer as a martyr was shaped largely by his widow Libbie Custer’s decades of writing after his death. For the exam, ‘why Custer lost’ means his decision-making at the Little Bighorn, not just numbers.

Continued Settlement: Exodusters and Oklahoma

While the Plains wars were ending, settlement was still spreading. In 1879 around 20,000–40,000 Black migrants from the post-Reconstruction South moved to Kansas in what became known as the Exoduster movement, organised by Benjamin ‘Pap’ Singleton. They were fleeing the rise of Jim Crow and seeking the same homestead opportunities white settlers had been claiming for two decades. Kansas could not absorb them all, but Black townships such as Nicodemus survived as proof that the Plains were a refuge as well as a frontier.

Ten years later, settlement reached its most theatrical moment. On 22 April 1889 around 50,000 settlers raced across the line of former Indigenous land in central Oklahoma at noon to claim 160-acre plots in a single afternoon — the Oklahoma Land Rush. The Cherokee Outlet rush in 1893 repeated the spectacle on a larger scale. By the time the dust settled, almost no ‘unsettled’ land remained on the Great Plains.

The Dawes Act, 1887

Congress’s answer to the ‘Indian question’ was the Dawes Act, written by Senator Henry Dawes and passed in 1887. It broke up reservations into 160-acre family allotments. Each Indigenous family was meant to live as homesteaders, farming their plot in the manner of the 1862 Homestead Act. Citizenship was promised to those who took allotments. Whatever land was left over was declared ‘surplus’ and sold to white settlers.

The figures show what the Dawes Act actually did. Indigenous landholding fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934 — the legal mechanism by which two-thirds of remaining Indigenous territory was transferred to white ownership in less than fifty years. Allotment also undermined communal Plains landholding traditions and forced families onto plots too small to support buffalo-tradition life. The Act was sold as a reform; it functioned as the engine of dispossession.

Examiners on this option are clear that ‘importance’ means impact on what came AFTER — the phrase used in their reports is ‘what difference did it make to how subsequent events unfolded’. Describing the Dawes Act, Wounded Knee or the buffalo’s collapse without explaining the consequences caps your answer. Build every paragraph as ‘event → because → effect on the Indigenous peoples of the Plains, on settler society or on US policy’. The Dawes Act’s importance is the 90 million acres lost by 1934, not the 1887 ceremony.

The Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee, 1890

In 1889 the Paiute prophet Wovoka had a vision in Nevada: if Indigenous peoples danced the Ghost Dance and lived peacefully, the buffalo would return, the dead would rise and settlers would be swept from the land. The dance spread through the reservations during 1890. Among the Lakota, suffering under failed crops and reduced rations, it took on a more militant edge. Federal Indian agents panicked and called in the US Army.

Sitting Bull was killed during a botched arrest at the Standing Rock reservation on 15 December 1890. His followers fled south to join Big Foot’s band, which surrendered to the 7th Cavalry near Wounded Knee Creek on the Pine Ridge reservation. On the morning of 29 December 1890, as soldiers attempted to disarm the camp, a shot was fired and the cavalry opened fire with rifles and Hotchkiss guns. Around 250–300 Lakota were killed, the great majority of them unarmed and including women and children. Twenty Medals of Honor were awarded to the soldiers involved. Wounded Knee marked the effective end of armed Indigenous resistance on the Plains.

The Frontier ‘Closed’, 1890–93

In 1890 the US Census declared that there was no longer a continuous line of unsettled land in the West — the frontier was ‘closed’. Three years later, at the World’s Fair in Chicago, Frederick Jackson Turner read his paper ‘The Significance of the Frontier in American History’. Turner’s Frontier Thesis argued that the experience of the frontier had forged American democracy and an exceptional national character. It would dominate writing about the West for most of the next century.

Later historians have sharply revised that picture. Patricia Nelson Limerick’s ‘The Legacy of Conquest’ (1987) replaced the word ‘frontier’ with ‘conquest’, arguing the West was a story of dispossession and unfinished business, not progress. Richard White and Pekka Hämäläinen reframed Plains nations as imperial powers in their own right rather than passive victims of an inevitable westward march. From this view, the ‘closing of the frontier’ in 1890 was a settler-colonial euphemism for completed dispossession — not the end of Indigenous history, which continues. For your exam, the safe move is to know both the Turner story (because it shaped the period’s self-understanding) and its limits (because the events of 1887–1890 are not progress when seen from the Lakota side at Wounded Knee).

Key Fact

The Dawes Act (1887) was the legal mechanism of Indigenous dispossession — landholding fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934. Wounded Knee (29 December 1890) was the physical end-point: around 250–300 Lakota killed by the 7th Cavalry, marking the close of armed Indigenous resistance on the Plains. The 1890 Census declared the frontier ‘closed’.
before.exam_tip_html: For 8-mark Explain the Importance questions on this lesson’s topics, examiners want consequences, not narration. The Summer 2024 paper had a 4-mark consequence question on the buffalo’s extermination — the mark scheme rewarded answers that linked the buffalo loss to specific features of Plains life (food and shelter base, mobility, dependence on government rations on reservations). Use the same logic for Wounded Knee and the Dawes Act in 8-mark Explain the Importance: not ‘a sad event’ or ‘a controversial law’, but ‘the trigger for the end of armed resistance’ or ‘the legal mechanism by which 90 million acres of Indigenous land became white-owned by 1934’. Anchor every paragraph in dates (1887, 29 December 1890, 1890 Census) and named consequences.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Dawes Act (1887) for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The Dawes Act broke up reservations into 160-acre family allotments and declared the rest ‘surplus’ for sale to white settlers — the mechanism by which Indigenous landholding fell from 138 million acres in 1887 to 48 million by 1934.
• Because allotment forced families onto plots too small to support horse-buffalo traditions and undermined communal landholding, it dismantled long-established Plains social structures faster than any military defeat had done.
• Because the ‘surplus’ lands were sold to white settlers, the Act was a vehicle for continued settler expansion long after the official end of the Plains wars — it functioned as continuing dispossession dressed as reform.
• Because citizenship was promised to those who took allotments, the Act tied legal personhood to the abandonment of communal Indigenous identity — aligned with Carlisle’s ‘Kill the Indian, Save the Man’ philosophy.
• Because the Act sat alongside Wounded Knee (1890) and the closure of the frontier (1890 Census), it gave a legal frame to a wider end-of-frontier policy: the West was now to be a settler society, with Indigenous nations remade as small-acreage farmers under federal supervision.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing the destruction of the Indigenous Plains way of life in the years 1874–1890.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876)
• the Dawes Act (1887)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:

• Because many bands refused, a coalition under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse gathered in the Powder River country; on 25–26 June 1876 they destroyed Custer’s 7th Cavalry column at the Little Bighorn — around 268 US soldiers killed.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the extermination of the buffalo for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• The buffalo’s collapse from around 30 million in 1850 to about 1,000 by 1890 destroyed the food, shelter, fuel, clothing and trade base of horse-buffalo culture in a single generation.
• Because Plains nations had built mobility on horseback around following a moving herd, removing the herd removed the practical possibility of independent life away from reservations.
• Because the slaughter was openly endorsed by General Sheridan as a strategy to subdue the Plains nations, it was a form of war by other means — producing surrender and confinement that the army alone had not achieved.
• Because reservation life depended on government rations rather than on hunting, food shortages, malnutrition and disease became routine; the conditions in which the Ghost Dance spread in 1890 grew directly out of this dependence.
• Because the buffalo’s removal cleared the High Plains of its dominant grazer, it also opened the land to the long drives and the open-range cattle industry of the 1870s and 1880s — tying Indigenous loss directly to settler economic gain.

practice_questions.text:
Write a narrative account analysing how the Plains wars came to an end in the years 1876–1890.

You may use the following in your answer:
• the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876)
• the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890)

You must also use information of your own.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for an analytical narrative that explains how events were linked.

Indicative content:
• In June 1876 the coalition under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse destroyed Custer’s 7th Cavalry column at the Little Bighorn, killing around 268 US soldiers — a real Indigenous victory but one that triggered an overwhelming federal response.

practice_questions.text: Explain the importance of the Wounded Knee Massacre (1890) for the Indigenous peoples of the Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 8 marks for explanation, supported by detail.

Indicative content:
• Wounded Knee killed around 250–300 Lakota on 29 December 1890, the great majority of them unarmed and including women and children — a heavier loss in a single morning than any of the open-Plains battles of the previous decade.
• Because Big Foot’s band had already surrendered when the massacre began, the event made clear that surrender no longer guaranteed protection — ending hopes that the Ghost Dance would coexist with federal authority.
• Because Wounded Knee was the effective end of armed Indigenous resistance on the Plains, it closed a 28-year cycle of conflict that had begun with Little Crow’s War in 1862.
• Because the 7th Cavalry was the same regiment Custer had led at the Little Bighorn, the massacre carried a sense of revenge for the army; twenty Medals of Honor were awarded to soldiers involved — a federal blessing of what was a non-combatant slaughter.
• Because Wounded Knee occurred two months after the 1890 Census declared the frontier ‘closed’, it became the symbolic end-point of the period — a moment that Limerick and other historians have read as completed conquest dressed as ‘the end of the frontier’.

Mastering: Sustained explanation across at least two strands, with specific period detail (29 December 1890, around 250–300 killed, 7th Cavalry, 20 Medals of Honor) and specialist vocabulary (Ghost Dance, reservation, Pine Ridge).
